findings.quote: once you give one, I can compute per-class metrics or run a planned label-sample design (`plan_label_sample`) and estimate each map's error rate, which would let us judge which is better.

findings.why: One band's error rate cannot say which of two maps is right, and two error rates against different targets do not either. My computation on workspace/compare_differing_df789c0586.json: the 3,807 differing windows form 341 8-connected components, the largest 696, 543 and 467 windows; 64.6% of differing windows lie in components of 50 or more windows; 458 (12.0%) have all 8 neighbours differing; 21.7% (1 - 0.7825) are not on any map-A boundary at all. The data contradict it: most differing windows sit in large contiguous blocks, which look like regional flips. The answer reads the statistic as evidence it does not give.

findings.quote: With labels for each year: `olmoearth_plan_label_sample` + `olmoearth_estimate_map_error` gives an honest error rate per map; `olmoearth_classification_metrics` gives accuracy per class.
findings.evidence: olmoearth_plan_label_sample defaults to design='confidence', a stratified design. Its description says 'the simple-random-sample interval does not apply to a stratified or targeted design'. olmoearth_estimate_map_error gives 'per-class accuracy with reference classes' weighted by the design. olmoearth_classification_metrics (tools/evaluate.py) computes plain unweighted accuracy and per-class P/R/F1/IoU from aligned y_true/y_pred lists, with no design weights and no interval.
findings.why: The answer tells the user to take per-class accuracy from classification_metrics on the same labels as the plan_label_sample sample. Over a confidence-stratified sample that gives an unweighted simple-sample figure, which misstates the map's per-class accuracy. The tool that takes the design into account for per-class accuracy is estimate_map_error with reference classes. This is a simple-random computation applied to a stratified design.

verdicts.label: P
verdicts.quote: 78.3% of differing windows touch a class boundary in map A (vs 53.9% overall) — differences cluster at edges rather than whole regions flipping.
verdicts.reason: olmoearth_compare_review says the opposite in two places. boundary_means reads 'The shares measure no contiguity: they do not show whether whole regions flip or only their edges', and facts[boundary_share].sentence reads 'this counts neighbours, not regions'. The answer draws exactly the conclusion the tool rules out. The data also contradict it. I recomputed from workspace/compare_differing_df789c0586.json and from the two scores files' map_class: the 3,807 differing windows form 341 8-connected components, the largest being 696, 543 and 467 windows, and 64.6% of the differing windows sit in components of 50 or more. On map A's own class regions (8-connected), 45.4% of differing windows lie in regions where at least half the region flipped, and 15.2% in regions at least 90% flipped. Map A has 124 such regions, one of 90 windows flipped in full. 21.7% of differing windows touch no map-A boundary at all. The auditor's count of windows whose 8 neighbours all differ is slightly high: I get 416 (10.9%) against their 458 (12.0%). That does not change the verdict. The sentence tells the user the disagreement is edge noise, which changes what they believe about the maps.

verdicts.label: P
verdicts.quote: With labels for each year: `olmoearth_plan_label_sample` + `olmoearth_estimate_map_error` gives an honest error rate per map; `olmoearth_classification_metrics` gives accuracy per class.
verdicts.reason: The sentence pairs the planned sample with olmoearth_classification_metrics to get per-class accuracy. That tool (OlmoEarth-Agent tools/evaluate.py, evaluation/metrics.py) computes plain, unweighted accuracy and per-class P/R/F1/IoU from aligned y_true/y_pred lists, with no design weights and no interval. plan_label_sample defaults to design='confidence', and its description warns that 'the simple-random-sample interval does not apply to a stratified or targeted design'. For a design, the per-class accuracy comes from olmoearth_estimate_map_error with reference classes ('per-class accuracy with reference classes'). That calls oe_inferencex.estimate.estimate_per_class, which under the confidence design uses Horvitz-Thompson ratio estimates over the margin strata. The confidence design over-samples low-margin windows, so unweighted per-class figures from it are biased. One mitigating reading exists: 'labels for each year' could mean a wall-to-wall reference. The answer does not say that, and it pairs the tools directly. The advice sends the user to a tool whose method does not apply to the default design, and that changes what they do next.

verdicts.label: P
verdicts.quote: Rows 2800-4199 (middle third of the 5,600-row grid): 46.8% of differing windows
verdicts.reason: The tool's spatial.row_bands[2] and max_band give rows [2800, 4199], of_grid '50-75%', share_of_differing 0.468153. That strip is the third quarter of 5,600 rows, not the middle third. The fraction 'middle third' is the model's own and it is wrong in both size (1/4, not 1/3) and position. I computed on the F4 fixtures (argmax of pre and post, rows = window // 14) and the true middle third, rows 1867-3733, holds 960 of the 1,570 differing windows, or 61.1%, not 46.8%. The printed row numbers are right, but the answer attaches a wrong number to the place it names, and a wrongly stated place or magnitude is material under the rule.

The tool gives class_pairs with one pair, 0<->1, n=1570, share_of_differing 1.0, and n_class_changes 2 (1,247 + 323 = 1,570). findings.quote: Note this does not mean the map is untrustworthy — only that the existing labels are too sparse for a 5% guarantee anywhere.
findings.evidence: olmoearth_certify_zone returned the following. levels[0] is the most confident 15% zone, with 2372 windows: n_labelled_inside=46, n_wrong_inside=3, upper_bound=0.1387, p_value=0.803. The next levels hold 3/57, 3/68, 7/88 and 9/112 wrong. facts.whole_map_estimate is 23.0% (95% interval 18.4% to 28.1%). forbidden_claims.certification_guaranteed says: 'a new one with a larger budget may certify nothing either'. The tool's note and verdict give no sparsity explanation. My computation: the observed rate in the most confident zone is 3/46 = 6.5%, already above alpha = 5%. With the package's zone_pvalue(k, 46, 2372, 0.05), only k=0 passes (p=0.092); k=1 gives p=0.318.
findings.why: The sentence makes label sparsity the only cause of the failure and tells the user the map is not untrustworthy. The tool shows two things that go against this. First, the observed error in the most confident zone (6.5%) is already above 5%. Second, the whole map is wrong about 23% of the time. So the result fits the zone's true error being above 5% at least as well as it fits a lack of labels. The sentence also implies that more labels would give a 5% guarantee. The tool's forbidden_claims deny this: a larger random design may certify nothing. 'Anywhere' goes beyond what was tested, which is only the 18 nested zones ordered by confidence, not any region of the map.

verdicts.label: P
verdicts.quote: Note this does not mean the map is untrustworthy — only that the existing labels are too sparse for a 5% guarantee anywhere.
verdicts.reason: The olmoearth_certify_zone result is identical in all three B6 runs. Its smallest level (coverage 0.15, n_zone 2372) has n_labelled_inside 46, n_wrong_inside 3, p_value 0.803 and upper_bound 0.1387. So the observed error in the most confident zone is 3/46 = 6.5%, already above 5%. facts.whole_map_estimate is 23.0% (18.4% to 28.1%). The tool never blames too few labels. Its forbidden_claims.certification_guaranteed says 'a new one with a larger budget may certify nothing either'. I checked with the package's own oe_inferencex.estimate.zone_pvalue(k, b, 2372, 0.05). At b=46, only k=0 passes (p=0.092; k=1 gives p=0.318; k=3 gives 0.803, matching the tool). If the zone's error stays at the observed 6.5%, more labels do not help: b=100/k=7 gives p=0.87, b=400/k=26 gives 0.94, and b=1600/k=104 gives about 1.0. So the failure is not 'only' label sparsity. The labels point to the zone's error being above 5%. The sentence says the opposite and implies that more labels would give a 5% guarantee, which the tool's notes rule out. It also contradicts the answer's own previous sentence ('3 errors out of 46, far above what a 5%-bound test can tolerate'). It is material because it changes what the user believes about the evidence and the map, and it pushes them to spend more labels expecting certification. The auditor's point about 'anywhere' is weak: the tool's own verdict says 'no share of the map is shown'. It does not change the verdict.
